headline: Houthis fire a missile at Saudi capital
summary: Saudi Arabia says Yemen's Houthi rebels fired a ballistic missile at Riyadh at dawn Saturday and that it was intercepted. Residents heard an explosion and later saw smoke near the airport. No casualties or damage were reported. It is the first Houthi attack on the capital since their fight opened a new front in the Iran war.

cover_question.q: Why would they shoot at a city?

cover_answer: Payback, they say, for Saudi strikes on Yemen.
table_question: If your friend gets in a fight, do you have to join in?

5-7.script: A group in Yemen fired a missile at a big city in Saudi Arabia, on the other side of the world. Saudi Arabia knocked it out of the sky before it landed, like a goalie blocking a shot. Some people saw smoke near the airport, and nobody was reported hurt. That is very far from here, and the grown-ups have it.
5-7.why: Hear "missile" and a five-year-old pictures it landing here. Say where it was, that it was blocked, and that nobody was hurt. They can't place Yemen on a map, so they read the danger off your face.
5-7.why_long: A five-year-old hears “missile” and pictures it here. That word is the story. Yemen and Riyadh do no work, and “far away” is not a distance they can feel, so the script hands them a goalie instead of a map. Joanne Cantor found young kids take fear from how a thing looks and sounds. Your face does more than the words.

8-12.chip: Bring it up if it fits the day
8-12.script: Yemen is in a civil war. Saudi Arabia backs one side, so the other side, the Houthis, fires missiles at Saudi cities. On Saturday one was aimed at the capital, Riyadh, and Saudi Arabia says it shot it down. Each block uses up an interceptor, and Saudi Arabia is running low, like a goalie low on gloves.
8-12.why: War, a backer, a strike back: a chain they can follow.
8-12.why_long: Ask a ten-year-old why and they want the chain, so the script gives them one. Civil war in Yemen, Saudi Arabia backs one side, so the other side hits Saudi cities. Same with the interceptor line: running out of what you use up is a rule they own. Expect “who started it” next. It goes back further than the headline.

13-17.script: If a country is running out of interceptors, who should send more? Saudi Arabia asked France, Britain, Pakistan and Egypt, not the US, after the Houthis aimed a missile at Riyadh. The US says it has no fight with them now. Wise, or a betrayal?
13-17.why: Teens can hold both: target and bomber, ally and bystander. Ask what they'd do first.
13-17.why_long: A teenager can hold two true things at once. Saudi Arabia is the target, and it has been bombing Yemen for years. So the script opens with a question and leaves it. Hand them your conclusion and you have told them the thinking is done, so they argue with that instead of the case. Ask what they’d do, then say what you think.

5-7.a: No. Saudi Arabia says it was knocked out of the sky. People saw smoke near the airport, and nobody was reported hurt.

8-12.q: Why would they shoot at a city?
8-12.a: Payback, they say, for Saudi strikes on Yemen. The two are at war.
The US says it has no fight with the Houthis now. Saudi Arabia asked France, Britain, Pakistan and Egypt for help.

13-17.a: Yemen's war goes back years. The Houthis say Saudi struck first.

13-17.q: Why does this move oil prices?
13-17.a: The Houthis hold Mokha and islands at the Red Sea's gate, on the Saudi oil route.
